title: Hot-take with Boz on frontier vs open models
power_dynamic: senior engineer-executive peer, external, blunt. Combative but fair, owns his own bias out loud, zero tolerance for opinions formed without doing the work. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Alright, give me your real take. Frontier models or open weights for what you're building, where do you actually land? And don't give me the both-have-tradeoffs answer.

What I'm building is a job, and the thing that needs to be done is much more specific and concrete. Pushing for frontier capabilities is not needed, and frontier capabilities are improving with different resources and different costs. For the voice agent, the one I have is much more specific, and from a budget and economics perspective, the open weights one works much better. That's what we're doing.

The cost argument for a narrow voice agent is real on paper. You save on compute and then you spend your engineering salaries fixing edge cases the frontier model handles out of the box. Did you actually run the total cost of ownership including the fine-tuning labor and pipeline drift, or are you just looking at inference bills?

You have hardness and evals to tune the whole thing, right? It's not just about the models. It's the hardness, the setup, the evaluations, and going back and configuring that. Even open weights here means I'm using an inference provider. I'm not looking through the lake of hosting it locally.

The harness and eval loop is the right way to build if you go open. That part is true. But the harness just eats the variance you saved in the model fee. You are shifting cost from the inference bill to the maintenance loop. Did you measure the velocity drop once the real user data starts breaking your evals?

Your hardware and eval are the crux of things. It does have a few reconfigurations, and you can swap the eval sets with a new model. That optionality is always a thing. There is always a risk, and you need to be ready with replacements.

Optionality sounds great until you realize you are spending half your sprint cycles swapping checkpoints instead of shipping features. You love the idea of dropping a new model in when it hits Hugging Face. Have you actually run the regression cost on your eval suite every time you swap, or is that optionality just a theoretical escape hatch?
I meant hardness and revals, not hardware.

Harness and evals, got it. You are still leaning on that harness to save you from underlying model drift. Optionality is a nice talking point until you are debugging why a prompt tweak broke your intent parser in production at two in the morning. Have you actually felt the burn of a full eval suite rewrite on a Friday night, or is this still just whiteboard architecture?
You will see when we get there.

That means no. You are betting the product on a theory you have not built yet. Do the work before you have an opinion. Have you actually shipped an open weights voice agent to production yourself, or are you just arguing from the design doc?

Do frontier models have the same sort of degradation when the next model comes or arrives? I am seeing a similar inference provider: a response that meets certain prompting and configuration instructions. It's such a limited capability that models released one year back by frontier can still do the job. The only difference here is the economics, the token rates. The one I'm using is exceptionally cheap and gets the job done.

The point about a narrow task needing only basic capabilities is real. The older frontier models handle it too. But if the capability threshold is that low, you are taking on open weights maintenance for a tiny margin on inference. Why not just pin an older frontier API version and avoid the pipeline tax entirely?
